entries.title: DAEMON
entries.body: A type of computer program that runs in the background, independently of user control. These programs perform tasks such as managing network services, monitoring systems, and responding to requests without requiring direct intervention. In the context of Bitcoin Core, the daemon is called "`bitcoind`". It is the version of Bitcoin Core without a user interface, which runs exclusively from the command line.

entries.title: DANDELION
entries.body:
A proposal that aims to improve the privacy of transaction routing in the Bitcoin network in order to counter deanonymization. In the classic operation of Bitcoin, transactions are immediately broadcast to multiple nodes. This can potentially allow observers to link transactions, which are normally anonymous, with IP addresses. The goal of BIP-0156 is to address this problem. To do so, it introduces an additional phase in the broadcast that preserves anonymity before public propagation. Thus, Dandelion first uses a "stem" phase in which the transaction is sent along a random path of nodes, before being broadcast to the entire network in the "fluff" phase. The stem and the fluff are references to the behavior of the transaction's propagation through the network, which resembles the shape of a dandelion ("*a dandelion*" in English). This routing method blurs the trail leading to the source node, making it difficult to trace a transaction through the network back to its origin.

![Dandelion graph: a linear stem from the source node in gray then fluff in a star shape toward the rest of the network.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/d/dandelion/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: DARKWALLET
entries.body: A privacy-focused Bitcoin wallet software launched by Amir Taaki and Cody Wilson in 2014, running as an extension for the Google Chrome browser. DarkWallet had features to improve the privacy of Bitcoin users, such as stealth payments and *coinjoins*. Its development has been abandoned since January 2015.

entries.title: DATABASE/
entries.body: A former folder containing databases for the Bitcoin Core wallet. Since version 0.16, this database has been moved into the `wallets/` folder.

entries.title: DB.LOG
entries.body: A former BDB (*BerkeleyDB*) error file of the Bitcoin Core wallet, moved into the `wallets/` folder since version 0.16.

entries.title: DBC
entries.body:
Acronym for "Deterministic Bitcoin Commitments". It is a set of rules for provably and uniquely embedding a commitment in a Bitcoin transaction. In the RGB protocol, there are two main forms of DBC:
* `Opret`;
* `Tapret`.

These mechanisms define precisely how the commitment is encoded in the outputs or in the structure of a Bitcoin transaction, in order to ensure that this commitment is detectable and verifiable in a deterministic way.

entries.title: DCA - DOLLAR COST AVERAGING
entries.body: An investment strategy that consists of investing a fixed amount of fiat currency in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of the asset's price. This method reduces the impact of volatility on the overall investment by buying more units when prices are low and fewer when they are high. DCA generally aims to build a position in an asset over the long term while minimizing risk. It is a very popular strategy for investing in bitcoin.

entries.title: DDOS
frenchAliases: ATTAQUE PAR DÉNI DE SERVICE DISTRIBUÉ
entries.body: A form of DOS where the attack comes from multiple sources simultaneously, making defense more complex. Attackers often use networks of computers infected with malware (botnets) to launch massive requests against a single target. This strategy multiplies the effectiveness of the attack by overloading the capacities of the targeted system in order to cause service interruptions.

entries.title: DEBUG.LOG
entries.body: A file containing the event history of Bitcoin Core. It contains logging data, such as error messages, warnings and other debugging information. This file is used to troubleshoot potential technical problems.

entries.title: DECENTRALIZATION
entries.body:
A principle of organization of a system in which no single entity holds control or authority over its overall operation. A decentralized system relies on a set of independent participants who collaborate according to common rules, with no single point of failure and no need to trust a central third party.

In Bitcoin, decentralization manifests itself at several levels. The network is composed of thousands of nodes spread across the world, each independently verifying transactions and blocks according to the protocol rules. Mining is carried out by many competing actors, and no miner can impose changes on its own. The development of the software is open and collaborative, with no single decision-making authority.

entries.title: DEFLATION
entries.body:
An economic phenomenon characterized by a general and lasting decline in the price level of goods and services. Unlike inflation, deflation means that the purchasing power of money increases over time: with the same amount of money, one can acquire more goods.

Deflation can result from a contraction of the money supply, an increase in productivity or a drop in demand. Keynesian economists generally consider it harmful, because it would encourage agents to postpone their purchases, thereby slowing economic activity. Economists of the Austrian school, however, distinguish monetary deflation (an artificial contraction of credit) from the fall in prices linked to productivity gains, the latter being seen as beneficial.

Bitcoin is often described as "deflationary" because of its supply capped at 21 million units and the gradual reduction of its issuance through *halvings*. More precisely, it is disinflationary: its issuance rate decreases over time and will converge toward zero.

entries.title: DEMURRAGE
entries.body:
A cost associated with holding a currency. By extension, demurrage sometimes refers to a monetary mechanism in which holding a currency for a prolonged period results in a penalty for its owner, for example by gradually decreasing its value. The goal is often to improve the velocity of circulation of the currency by discouraging long-term saving.

This mechanism is sometimes proposed to be implemented on Bitcoin in order to support the transaction fee market and to distribute the costs of the system more fairly. Indeed, the operating cost of Bitcoin will eventually rest solely on those who make transactions, and not on savers who nevertheless benefit from the security of the system. However, demurrage is very widely rejected by the Bitcoin community, because it penalizes long-term holders and is not consistent with the store-of-value characteristic of BTC. Since it imposes a gradual loss of value, it can be perceived as an infringement of the right to own property.

One could argue against demurrage by explaining that the cost of the current system already inevitably rests on savers, given that they had to make a transaction at some point to obtain their bitcoins. Moreover, the security of a given UTXO increases greatly with the first blocks after its creation, but over time, the additional security gained with each block becomes more and more marginal. Thus, it is not necessarily unfair not to make long-term holders bear the cost of mining.

Demurrage has notably been applied on the altcoin Freicoin, a fork of Bitcoin that implemented a system of negative interest rates.

entries.title: DEPEG
entries.body: Refers to the situation where the value of a digital asset, typically an IOU, becomes detached from the underlying asset to which it is normally pegged, thus causing price fluctuations relative to that asset. This phenomenon is particularly observed with *stablecoins*, designed to maintain a strict parity with fiat currencies or other reference assets. A *depeg* can also occur in the case of representations of bitcoins on *sidechains* or ETFs, where, in the event of a problem, the nominal value can diverge from that of bitcoin.

entries.title: DER
DERIVATION
DGM
entries.body: Acronym for "*Double Geometric Method*". It is a method for calculating miner rewards in the context of mining pools. DGM is a hybrid method, meant to combine the advantages of PPLNS and of the so-called "geometric" method. It has low variance on shares, in the manner of PPLNS, and then allows the pool operator to absorb part of the variance risk in a second step. DGM is resistant to *pool hopping* by ensuring that the expected payout per share remains constant. The method is based on scores, making payouts independent of the pool's history and almost entirely independent of future difficulty changes.

entries.title: DIFFICULTY
entries.body: An adjustable parameter that determines the complexity of the proof of work required to add a new block to the blockchain and earn the associated reward. This difficulty is represented by the difficulty target, a 256-bit value that sets the upper limit that the hash of a block header must respect to be considered valid. The goal is for the hash, computed through a double execution of `SHA256` (`SHA256d`), to be less than or equal to this target. To reach this hash, miners manipulate the `nonce` in the block header. The difficulty adjusts every 2016 blocks, or approximately every two weeks, to keep the average block creation time at about 10 minutes.

entries.title: DIFFIE-HELLMAN
entries.body: A cryptographic method allowing two parties to generate a shared secret over an insecure communication channel. This secret can then be used to encrypt the communication between the two parties. Diffie-Hellman uses modular arithmetic so that, even if an attacker can observe the exchanges, they cannot deduce the shared secret without solving a hard mathematical problem: the discrete logarithm. On Bitcoin, a variant of DH using an elliptic curve named ECDH is sometimes used, notably for static address protocols such as *Silent Payments* or BIP-0047.

entries.title: DIGICASH
entries.body: Company founded in 1989 by the cryptographer David Chaum, which was a pioneer in the field of anonymous electronic payments. DigiCash developed the eCash system, a digital money protocol based on the blind signatures invented by Chaum. This mechanism allowed a bank to issue digital tokens without being able to trace the transactions made by users, thus guaranteeing anonymity comparable to that of cash. Despite trials with several banks, notably Mark Twain Bank in the United States and Deutsche Bank, the system failed to achieve sufficient adoption. DigiCash went bankrupt in 1998. The eCash concept is considered an important precursor to Bitcoin, notably for its approach to privacy in digital payments.

entries.title: DIGITAL ARTIFACTS
entries.body: In the context of the Ordinals protocol, this is a sat that has been inscribed with specific data through the inscription mechanism. These artifacts can include images, texts, or any other type of digital content and are inseparably linked to the corresponding satoshi.

entries.title: DIRECTED ACYCLIC GRAPH
entries.body: A DAG is a mathematical structure made up of nodes interconnected by directed edges, without forming a cycle, which allows a rigorous topological ordering. In the RGB protocol, the DAG is used to represent the structure of contract *Shards*, for the management and verification of state transitions. This graph representation makes it possible to ensure the consistency and traceability of modifications in a distributed environment.

entries.title: DISTRIBUTED
entries.body:
Attribute of a computer network in which decision-making power and control are shared equitably among all participants in the network. This distribution guarantees the resilience of the system. It is also called a peer-to-peer network. Unlike a decentralized network, where power is fragmented and dispersed among several entities, but where some central authorities remain endowed with greater power than the users, a distributed network eliminates the central authority by entrusting management and control to the users themselves. Bitcoin is an example of a distributed system. Bitcoin has no hierarchy or central authority. Maintaining consensus, verifying transactions, and issuing new monetary units are carried out by the users. This distributed structure ensures the system's resilience and resistance to censorship, making it very difficult for a single entity to control or manipulate it.

*Some people speak of Bitcoin as a decentralized system. Indeed, it is not uncommon to see these two terms used interchangeably. A more evocative synonym for the adjective “distributed” could be “peer-to-peer”, sometimes abbreviated “P2P”, the acronym of the English “Peer-to-Peer”.*

entries.title: DKG
entries.body: Type of protocol that allows a set of n participants to collectively generate a cryptographic key pair, without relying on a trusted third party and without any participant knowing the complete private key. Each participant obtains a share of the private key, while the common public key is accessible to everyone. The acronym “DKG” stands for *Distributed Key Generation*.

entries.title: DLC - DISCREET LOG CONTRACT
entries.body: Type of smart contract on Bitcoin that allows contractual conditions to be executed based on the outcome of external events, validated by one or more oracles, without the latter knowing the details of the contract. DLCs were invented by Tadge Dryja in 2017. These smart contracts are mainly useful in financial applications, making it possible, for example, to create financial instruments or conditional bets, while reducing counterparty risk. To build a DLC, several parties lock bitcoins on a multisig address. These bitcoins can only be unlocked when the oracle publishes the specified information at a given time.

entries.title: DLP - DISCRETE LOGARITHM PROBLEM
entries.body: The discrete logarithm problem (DLP) is a mathematical problem on which the security of public-key cryptographic algorithms relies, notably those used on Bitcoin. In a cyclic group of order `q`, with a generator `g`, if we have an equation of the form `g^x = h`, then `x` is called the discrete logarithm of `h` with respect to the base `g`, modulo `q`. In simple terms, it consists of determining the exponent `x` when `g`, `h`, and `q` are known. The discrete logarithm is therefore the inverse of exponentiation in a finite cyclic group. However, for large values of `q`, solving the discrete logarithm problem is considered algorithmically hard. This property is exploited to ensure the security of many cryptographic protocols, such as the Diffie-Hellman protocol for key exchange. The discrete logarithm is also used in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC), among others in the ECDSA algorithm (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*). In the context of elliptic curves, the discrete logarithm problem extends to finding a scalar `k` such that `k \cdot G = K`, where `G` and `K` are points on the curve, and `\cdot` represents the point multiplication operation. In the context of Bitcoin, standard transactions use either ECDSA or the Schnorr protocol in order to lock UTXOs. Both rely on the impossibility of computing the discrete logarithm.

entries.title: DNS SEEDS
DOJO
entries.body: *Open source* *backend* server built on top of Bitcoin Core, oriented toward privacy and autonomy. Initially developed by the Samourai Wallet teams, the Dojo project is now maintained by the community. Dojo serves as a gateway between a Bitcoin wallet (such as Ashigaru) and the Bitcoin network, making it possible to query blockchain data and broadcast transactions through its own infrastructure. It includes Bitcoin Core, the Fulcrum indexer, and the BTC-RPC Explorer.

entries.title: DOS - DENIAL OF SERVICE
entries.body: Cyberattack that aims to make a resource (website, node, online service...) unavailable to its legitimate users. Attackers overload the target with an excessively high volume of data or requests, which exhausts the victim's system and network resources, causing slowdowns or a complete shutdown. DoS methods can vary, but the objective remains the same: to prevent access to services or data. In the specific context of Bitcoin, a DoS attack can aim to saturate the network or nodes with an excessive volume of requests in order to hinder their normal operation. The objective is often to harm a node operator or the availability of the network for honest users.

entries.title: DOUBLE SPENDING ATTACK
entries.body:
Attack in which a malicious user attempts to use the same UTXO (*Unspent Transaction Output*) more than once in order to enrich themselves at the expense of the counterparties of the transactions involved. In principle, once a transaction is confirmed in a block and added to the blockchain, the use of those bitcoins is permanently recorded, preventing any later spending of those same bitcoins. Preventing double spending is even the primary purpose of the blockchain. 

In a double spending attack, the attacker first makes a legitimate transaction to a merchant, then creates a second, competing transaction that spends the same coins, either by sending them back to themselves to recover the amount, or by using them to buy another good or service from another merchant. 

Two main scenarios can enable this attack. The first, and the simplest for the attacker, consists of executing the fraudulent transaction before the legitimate transaction is included in a block. To get their fraudulent transaction confirmed first, the attacker attaches to it significantly higher transaction fees than the legitimate transaction. It is a sort of fraudulent RBF. This scenario is only possible if the merchant agrees to finalize the sale with “zeroconf”, that is, with no confirmation at all for the payment transaction. This is why it is strongly recommended to wait for several confirmations before considering a transaction as immutable. The second scenario, much more complex, is that of a 51% attack. If the attacker controls a significant share of the network's computing power, they can mine a chain competing with the one containing the legitimate transaction, but including their fraudulent transaction. Once the merchant has accepted the sale and the attacker has managed to create a longer chain (with more accumulated work) than the legitimate chain, they can then broadcast their fraudulent chain, which will be recognized by the network's nodes as the valid one.

entries.title: DOXXIC CHANGE
entries.body:
Change output resulting from a *Tx0* transaction in the *Whirlpool* protocol, which represents a risk to the user's privacy. The *doxxic change* is the fraction of bitcoins that cannot be integrated into the chosen coinjoin pool and that returns to the wallet as change.

This change is described as “doxxic” (a portmanteau of “*toxic*” and “*doxx*”, that is, to expose someone's identity) because it retains a direct link to the *Tx0*, and therefore potentially to the user's identity or history. If this change is spent carelessly, for example by merging it with *postmix* UTXOs, it can compromise the privacy gained during the coinjoin cycles.

To limit this risk, the *doxxic change* can be spent separately (for example on gift cards, through donations, or on *Lightning*), used in a new *Tx0*, or consolidated via *atomic swaps* on Monero.

entries.title: DRIVECHAIN
entries.body: Specific form of sidechain where the miners of the main blockchain (Bitcoin) have a direct role in the governance of the two-way peg and possibly in the sidechain's consensus mechanism. This protocol was invented by Paul Sztorc and could be put in place thanks to the controversial BIP-0300, which would enable the *two-way peg* with miners, and BIP-0301, which would enable the use of blind merged mining (*Blind Merged Mining*).

entries.title: DUAL FUNDING
entries.body:
When opening a Lightning channel, *dual funding* allows both participants to lock bitcoins in it. Unlike the traditional model where a single node funds the channel, this method allows both parties to fund it, which makes it possible to balance its liquidity immediately.

*Dual funding* is included in version 2 of the channel construction protocol, which uses a negotiation phase. The two parties collaborate to create the funding transaction by exchanging messages to add or remove bitcoins until the transaction is finalized.

entries.title: DUMMY ELEMENT
entries.body: Refers to an additional, useless element consumed by the opcodes `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` and `OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY` when verifying signatures in a transaction. Because of a historical *off-by-one* bug (unit offset error), these 2 opcodes remove an extra element from the stack in addition to their basic function. To avoid an error, it is therefore mandatory to include a dummy value at the beginning of the `scriptSig` in order to satisfy the removal and bypass the bug. This useless value is what is called the “*dummy element*”. BIP-0011, which introduced the P2MS standard, advised putting a `OP_0` as the useless value. But this standard was not enforced at the consensus rule level, which means that any value could be placed there without invalidating the transaction. The dummy element was therefore a vector of transaction malleability. BIP-0147, introduced with the SegWit soft fork, required this dummy element to be strictly an empty byte array (`OP_0`), thus eliminating the malleability associated with this element by making any non-compliant transaction invalid under the consensus rules. This rule, named `NULLDUMMY`, applies to both SegWit and pre-SegWit transactions.

entries.title: DURESS WALLET
entries.body:
Secondary wallet designed to offer plausible deniability in case of physical coercion. When a user is forced to unlock their *signing device* under threat (a scenario known as a “*$5 wrench attack*”), they enter a special PIN called a “duress PIN” that opens a wallet containing a reduced amount. The attacker cannot determine whether another wallet exists on the device.

The *duress wallet* derives from a seed or a derivation path distinct from that of the main wallet. Its interface and operation are identical, which makes it impossible to tell the two apart. On some *signing devices* such as the Coldcard, this feature relies on a dedicated PIN; on other devices, the BIP-0039 passphrase fulfills a similar role by giving access to an entirely different wallet depending on the passphrase entered.

The principle assumes maintaining a credible balance in the *duress wallet* so that the decoy is convincing.

entries.title: DUST
entries.body: Refers to extremely small amounts of bitcoin coins that are too tiny to be sent in a transaction, because the transaction fees needed to include them in a block would be proportionally higher than their value. The precise definition of “dust” can vary depending on the context, but it is generally any transaction output that requires more fees to be spent than the value it holds. For the Bitcoin user, it is important to manage their UTXOs and to practice consolidating them so that they do not become dust.

entries.title: DUST LIMIT
entries.body: Refers to the threshold in sats below which a UTXO is considered “dust” (*dust*) by a node on the network. This threshold is part of the standardness rules, which can be modified independently by each node. In Bitcoin Core, this limit is determined by a specific fee rate, set by default at 3,000 sats per virtual kilobyte (sats/kvB). This limit aims to restrict the propagation of transactions containing very small amounts of bitcoin. Indeed, a UTXO classified as dust implies that using it is not economically rational: spending this UTXO would cost more than simply abandoning it. If spending dust is not rational, this suggests that such spending can only be motivated by external incentives, often malicious. This can notably be a problem if a malicious actor seeks to saturate the network with transactions containing tiny amounts, with the aim of increasing the operational load on nodes and potentially preventing them from processing other legitimate transactions. To give an analogy (a somewhat shaky one, I admit), it is a bit like someone trying to pay for a €100 grocery basket solely with 1-cent coins in order to block the other customers at the checkout.

entries.title: DUSTING ATTACK
entries.body:
Attack that consists of sending tiny amounts of bitcoin to a large number of receiving addresses. The attacker's objective is to push the recipients to pool these amounts with other UTXOs. The attacker then tracks the future movements of these small amounts of bitcoin, with the aim of forming address *clusters*, that is, determining whether several addresses belong to the same entity. By cross-referencing the information gathered during a dusting attack with other data and heuristics used in chain analysis, it is possible for the attacker to identify certain entities and their associated addresses. This method represents a threat only to users' privacy, but does not affect the security of their funds.

*Some bitcoiners suggest no longer using the term “dusting attack” because it would be misleading. Indeed, the term “dust” describes something quite specific in Bitcoin Core. If the dusting attack actually used dust as described in Core, the attack would be ineffective. Some therefore suggest using the term “forced address reuse” to describe this attack more precisely.*

entries.title: DUSTRELAYFEE
entries.body:
Standardness rule used by network nodes to determine what they consider the "dust limit". This parameter sets a fee rate in sats per virtual kilobyte (sats/kvB) that serves as a reference for calculating whether the value of a UTXO is lower than the fees needed to include it in a transaction. Indeed, a UTXO is considered "dust" on Bitcoin if it requires more fees to be spent than the value it represents itself. The calculation of this limit is as follows:

```text
limite = (taille entrée + taille sortie) * taux de frais
```

Since the fee rate required for a transaction to be included in a Bitcoin block constantly varies, the `DustRelayFee` parameter makes it possible to define the fee rate used in this calculation by each node. By default, on Bitcoin Core, this value is set to 3,000 sats/kvB. For example, to calculate the dust limit of a P2PKH input and output, which measure 148 and 34 bytes respectively, the calculation would be: 

```text
limite (sats) = (148 + 34) * 3000 / 1000 = 546 sats
```

This means that the node in question will not relay transactions including a UTXO secured with P2PKH whose value is lower than 546 sats.

entries.title: DYNAFED - DYNAMIC FEDERATIONS
entries.body: Governance mechanism deployed on the Liquid network that makes it possible to change the composition of the federation of functionaries without interrupting the operation of the network. Before the introduction of Dynamic Federations (DynaFed), any change to the list of block signers or watchmen (*watchmen*) required manual coordination and a network interruption. DynaFed was activated on Liquid in October 2021 through a *hard fork*.

entries.title: HARDENED DERIVATION
entries.body: A process for generating child keys in HD wallets. Hardened derivation uses the parent private key as input to the `HMAC-SHA512` function, which makes it impossible to generate child public keys from the parent public key and the parent chain code. The process involves concatenating the parent private key and an index greater than or equal to `2^{31}`, followed by applying `HMAC-SHA512` with the parent chain code. The result is split into two parts: the first 256 bits are added to the parent private key to obtain the child private key, while the remaining 256 bits form the child chain code. This method ensures that even if an extended public key is compromised, it cannot be used to derive the child public keys. In a standard derivation, hardened derivation is used at all derivation levels down to the account depth. In derivation path notations, a hardened derivation is identified with an apostrophe `'` or, more rarely, with a `h`.

entries.title: MONETARY DARWINISM
entries.body:
A concept that applies Darwin's theory of natural selection to the monetary domain. It postulates that the different forms of money compete with one another and that the currencies with the best-suited properties (scarcity, durability, divisibility, portability, fungibility, verifiability) eventually supplant those that perform less well.

From this perspective, proponents of this concept see Bitcoin as a superior currency likely to prevail over fiat currencies through the sheer strength of its intrinsic properties. Its strictly limited supply, its censorship resistance and its decentralized nature would constitute decisive competitive advantages in this monetary selection.

This concept is closely linked to that of hyperbitcoinization and follows in the tradition of Thiers' law (good money drives out bad), in opposition to Gresham's law (bad money drives out good).

entries.title: NORMAL DERIVATION
entries.body: A process for generating child keys in HD wallets. Normal derivation uses the parent public key as input to the `HMAC-SHA512` function, which makes it possible to generate child public keys from the parent public key and the parent chain code. The process involves concatenating the parent public key and an index lower than `2^{31}`, followed by applying `HMAC-SHA512` with the parent chain code. The result is split into two parts: the first 256 bits are added to the parent private key to obtain the child private key, while the remaining 256 bits form the child chain code. This method ensures that the extended public key can be used to derive the child public keys. In a standard derivation, normal derivation is used at all derivation levels from the account depth onward. In derivation path notations, a normal derivation is identified when there is just the index without any apostrophe `'`.

entries.title: PLAUSIBLE DENIABILITY
entries.body:
A principle according to which a user can credibly deny possessing or controlling certain bitcoins, because there are several plausible interpretations of a given situation. In the context of Bitcoin, plausible deniability is a goal sought by many privacy techniques.

For example, a coinjoin transaction offers plausible deniability because an observer cannot prove with certainty which output belongs to which participant. If a user is asked whether they own a particular UTXO resulting from a coinjoin, they can credibly deny it, since several participants could be its owner.

Similarly, a hidden wallet (*hidden wallet*) protected by a BIP-0039 passphrase offers plausible deniability. A user under duress can reveal their recovery phrase without the passphrase, giving access to a decoy wallet, while denying the existence of the hidden wallet associated with the secret passphrase.

Plausible deniability is a key concept for the protection of privacy and the physical security of bitcoin holders, particularly against state or criminal adversaries.

entries.title: PROPAGATION / BROADCAST
entries.body: Process by which information, such as transactions and blocks, is passed from node to node across the Bitcoin network. When a user makes a transaction, it is first verified by the node they are connected to. After validation, this transaction is relayed to the other nodes connected to that node, which in turn verify it and then propagate it. Quickly, a large share of the nodes on the network will be aware of the transaction. If it offers enough fees, miners will include it in their candidate block. When a block containing this transaction is validated, the transaction is then confirmed.

entries.title: REPOSITORY / REPO
entries.body: A central data structure used in Git where a project's versioning information is stored. A repository contains the complete history of all changes, branches and tags. Each repository is an independent collection of files and folders, accompanied by a history of commits, enabling collaboration and tracking of changes over time. For example, the Bitcoin Core repository is stored on GitHub here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin.
